content: Hereditary ataxias represent a diverse group of disorders characterized by progressive loss of coordination. One of the common and potentially life-threatening complications of these conditions is swallowing impairment, medically referred to as dysphagia. Dysphagia can significantly compromise an individual’s health and overall well-being, as the inability to swallow effectively and safely can lead to serious consequences such as malnutrition, dehydration, and aspiration pneumonia. Addressing difficulties with eating and drinking is therefore a critical aspect of clinical care for individuals with hereditary ataxia. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various interventions aimed at managing dysphagia in individuals with hereditary ataxias. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL Plus, PsycINFO, and ERIC, on September 14, 2015. Additional searches were performed in Linguistics and Language Behavior Abstracts (LLBA), Dissertation Abstracts, and Trials Registries on September 24, 2015. The inclusion criteria for this review were strict, focusing solely on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared dysphagia treatments in hereditary ataxia patients with either placebo or no treatment. Only studies that specifically measured swallowing impairment were considered eligible for inclusion. Three independent reviewers meticulously screened all titles and abstracts, and any disagreements or uncertainties regarding study inclusion were resolved through consensus. From the 519 titles and abstracts screened, no RCTs or quasi-RCTs were identified that met the inclusion criteria. Many studies were excluded because they did not involve participants with hereditary ataxia, focused on other neurological conditions, were theoretical reviews rather than intervention studies, or were not randomized or quasi-randomized trials. However, five studies of various designs were identified that described treatments for dysphagia or reported improvements in swallowing as a secondary outcome in individuals with hereditary ataxia. Importantly, none of these studies were RCTs or quasi-RCTs. The authors concluded that there is currently no robust evidence to support the use of any specific intervention for managing dysphagia in hereditary ataxia. This lack of evidence underscores the urgent need for well-designed, controlled clinical trials to investigate effective treatments for swallowing impairments in this patient population.
